solution: The number of potatoes never changes, so Red's score is exactly the number of potatoes standing on even seats when the bell rings and Blue's is the number on odd seats; the game is zero-sum in that count. Inside a maximal block of consecutive potatoes only the clockwise-most one can move, and its current holder wants it on the opposite parity — but passing early hands the potato to the opposing team, which can then simply sit on it until the bell, and it also unblocks the potato behind it. Keeping everything and passing only in the final round is therefore a dominant plan for both sides, so the outcome is: the head of every maximal circular run of potatoes advances exactly one seat (nothing moves at all if the circle is completely full), and the answer is the parity split of that configuration. This is independent of k, giving O(n) per test. Exhaustive game search over all states for 2n <= 8 and k in {1,2,3,5} reproduced this rule and found a pure equilibrium in every state, and all six samples match.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force
notes: Verified by exhaustive minimax over the simultaneous-move game (2n <= 8, k in {1,2,3,5}); a pure equilibrium existed in every state, so the simultaneity is not essential. The whole problem is parity: team membership is seat parity, the score counts potatoes on the opposite parity, and every pass flips a potato's parity — hence parity-argument. greedy covers the dominant-move argument (CF tags it greedy) but the reasoning is really a dominance/exchange argument. Deliberately not labelled simulation: k is up to 1e9 and the final state is computed in one pass over the runs, never simulated.
